title: Replace the Supreme Judicial Council and elect a new, independent Prosecutor General
description: Progressive Bulgaria's 2026 platform made the election of a new Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), whose mandate had expired, its main concrete institutional proposal, as the step that would allow the acting Prosecutor General to be replaced (OSW, April 2026). Opening his first cabinet meeting on 8 May 2026, Radev said the government would work 'together with the National Assembly in the election of a new, independent and legitimate Prosecutor General' and that judicial reform would not be limited to replacing the Prosecutor General.
reasoning: Parliament amended the Judicial System Act in June 2026 to set the procedure for electing the new SJC, bar former supreme court presidents and prosecutors general of the outgoing council from membership, cap acting terms of the Prosecutor General and the supreme court presidents at six months in total, and require the SJC to hold the magistrates' elections by 17 October 2026. The prosecutors' general assembly opened on 17 October with the vote set for 24 October, and the judges and investigating magistrates vote in October–November; the parliamentary quota needs a two-thirds majority (160 of 240 MPs), which Progressive Bulgaria's 131 seats do not provide alone. Justice Minister Nikolay Naydenov expects the new SJC by mid-November 2026 and a Prosecutor General by early spring 2027. As of October 2026 neither has yet been elected.
key_evidence: OSW (10 April 2026): a new SJC is 'one of the few concrete proposals' of the PB platform; it would allow the replacement of the prosecutor general serving in an acting capacity

Borislav Sarafov resigned as acting Prosecutor General on 22 April 2026, three days after the election and before the government took office; Deputy Prosecutor General Vanya Stefanova was appointed acting Prosecutor General
26 June 2026: final amendments to the Judicial System Act set 17 October 2026 as the deadline for the professional-quota elections and a six-month cumulative cap on acting terms
17 October 2026: the general assembly of prosecutors opened the election of its SJC members (25 candidates), with voting on 24 October

10 September 2026: Justice Minister Naydenov expects the SJC by mid-November and a Prosecutor General by early spring 2027; talks with Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, not GERB, on the parliamentary quota

title: Keep a liberal fiscal framework: the 10% flat income tax and a low budget deficit
description: According to OSW's analysis of the platform, Progressive Bulgaria pledged to maintain a liberal fiscal framework, including the 10% flat income tax, a low budget deficit and tax relief for businesses, alongside higher wages and lower inequality. On 8 May 2026 Radev asked ministers to bring 'the unseen deficit, covered up expenses, unsettled invoices' to light before the budget was drafted.
reasoning: Tax rates were kept: the 2026 budget did not change them and Finance Minister Galab Donev said in September 2026 that the 2027 budget would keep tax rates at their current levels, while adding revenue measures (higher tobacco excise and vignette fees, personal social security contributions for civil servants and magistrates, a higher maximum contributory income and a one-off windfall levy in 2027). The deficit was not low: the budget adopted on 24 July 2026 set a deficit of 5.7% of GDP with up to EUR 10.1 billion of new borrowing, after the EU Council opened an excessive deficit procedure on 10 July 2026; the 2027 draft budgetary plan targets 4.3% and correction by 2029. The government attributes the deficit to obligations inherited from previous governments; Radev said going straight to 3% was not possible.
key_evidence: 24 July 2026: 2026 State Budget Act adopted 125–84 with a 5.7% deficit, a EUR 10.1 billion borrowing ceiling (up to EUR 3.261 billion under the EU SAFE instrument) and a 10% cut in personnel spending from 1 September
June 2026, Radev: 'There is no money in the treasury'; 'There is no way to move from such a high deficit to 3% immediately, and certainly not with little or no debt'
10 July 2026: the EU Council opened an excessive deficit procedure for Bulgaria
25 September 2026, Donev: measures for 2027 include 'keeping tax rates at their current levels'

15 October 2026: 2027 draft budgetary plan with a 4.3% deficit target, a one-off windfall contribution (indicative EUR 800 million) and a maximum contributory income of EUR 2,400 from 1 January 2027; 2026 accrual deficit now expected at about 5% of GDP

title: Curb price rises with tougher competition and consumer-protection rules, without price ceilings
description: On 8 May 2026, the day his government took office, Radev said bills to curb price growth would be submitted to parliament the following Monday. He ruled out a price ceiling but pledged to expose pricing processes, impose higher sanctions for unfair competition and protect Bulgarian producers from 'the arm-twisting practices of large retail chains'.
reasoning: Progressive Bulgaria MPs tabled amendments to the Protection of Competition Act and the Consumer Protection Act, and both were adopted at final reading on 11 June 2026. They ban 'excessively high' prices by undertakings in a monopoly or (collective) dominant position, with fines of up to 10% of turnover, shift the burden of proof to firms with at least 50% (or jointly 60%) market share, create an electronic register tracing agri-food supply chains, and extend until August 2027 the ban on 'economically unjustified' consumer price increases with higher fines. The legislative commitment was delivered as described; its effect on prices is disputed: Democratic Bulgaria said after 100 days that the promise to control prices had not been fulfilled, and Finance Minister Donev said in October 2026 that the measures would be felt 'in the long run', amid fuel price rises linked to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
key_evidence: 8 May 2026: Radev announces bills to curb price growth, 'no price ceiling'
11 June 2026: Protection of Competition Act amendments adopted; CPC fines of up to 10% of the previous year's turnover for excessive prices

11 June 2026: Consumer Protection Act amendments, passed with the votes of Progressive Bulgaria and the MRF, extend the ban on unjustified price increases to August 2027 and require large traders (turnover above EUR 25 million) to publish prices daily
16 August 2026: Democratic Bulgaria says the cabinet has not fulfilled its promise to control prices
4 October 2026: Donev says curbing prices is 'a difficult process' and the measures 'will be felt in the long run'

title: Save the Recovery and Resilience Plan funds at risk (over EUR 400 million)
description: At his first cabinet meeting on 8 May 2026 Radev listed 'the saving of the funds under the Recovery and Resilience Plan' among the government's priorities, and told reporters that his team would use bills already tabled, with its own amendments, to save over EUR 400 million under tight deadlines.
reasoning: The Act on Counteracting Corruption among Persons Holding Public Office, an RRP milestone tabled by the caretaker cabinet, was adopted under urgent procedure at the end of May 2026, ahead of the 5 June promulgation deadline. The European Commission approved 23 of the 26 milestones of Bulgaria's fourth payment request (about EUR 1.1 billion) and transferred EUR 896 million on 31 July 2026, with the remainder tied to outstanding reforms (water-sector legislation, a cultural-sector target, a public transport milestone). A separate suspension of EUR 118.4 million (24 July 2026) was still in its six-month correction period for two milestones. The fifth and final request (almost EUR 1.7 billion) was due by 30 September and payments must be made by 31 December 2026, so how much is saved will only be known then.
key_evidence: 14 May 2026: the anti-corruption bill was fast-tracked 'to safeguard payments under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan' (deadline for promulgation: 5 June)
18–19 June 2026: positive preliminary assessment of the fourth request, 23 of 26 milestones met
31 July 2026: EUR 896 million transferred; total received EUR 6.17 billion, 68% of the planned funding
October 2026 (Novinite, citing the Commission's report): suspension of EUR 118.4 million decided on 24 July 2026 lifted for one milestone, correction period running for two
All member states submitted final payment requests by 30 September 2026; final payments due by 31 December 2026

title: Audit every ministry for hidden deficits, problematic contracts and overstaffing, and slim down the administration
description: On 8 May 2026 Radev instructed each minister to make a detailed analysis of their portfolio 'within a short time', with an emphasis on finances and on whether problematic contracts, overstaffing and public procurement problems exist, so that the budget could be drawn up on that basis. The 2026–2030 governance programme adopted on 12 August 2026 schedules a 'structural and functional optimization' of the public administration for 2026–2027.
reasoning: The 2026 budget cut personnel spending by 10% from 1 September 2026 (with exemptions for municipalities, the military, the Interior Ministry, security services and others), reduced the boards of public enterprises from five to three members and stopped performance bonuses for heads of single-person state bodies. The 2027 draft budgetary plan says the structural spending cuts and administrative optimisation launched in 2026 will be completed in 2027, and the restructuring of the Road Infrastructure Agency cuts 505 positions in the National Toll Administration and some 85–87 in regional road administrations. This research found no consolidated published report on the ministry audits themselves; Continue the Change argues the changes amount to a replacement of personnel rather than reform.
key_evidence: 8 May 2026: ministers ordered to analyse their portfolios for 'problematic contracts, overstaffing and public procurement'
24 July 2026: 2026 budget provides a 10% reduction in personnel expenditure from 1 September
12 August 2026: governance programme schedules administrative optimisation for 2026–2027 and civil-service reform for 2028–2029
15 October 2026: optimisation 'launched this year' to be completed in 2027
22 October 2026: Road Infrastructure Agency reform in two stages; 505 National Toll Administration positions cut

title: End the supply of weapons from Bulgarian army stocks to Ukraine
description: As President, Radev opposed Bulgarian military support for Kyiv (OSW). On 10 June 2026, at the start of a cabinet meeting, he announced that the government was 'putting an end to the provision of weapons from the Bulgarian army to Ukraine': 'We have already given enough', calling instead for a diplomatic solution to the war.
reasoning: No further state supplies from army depots were made: Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said Ukraine had made no request to his ministry since 8 May 2026 and that stocks were already below the minimum. On 21 October 2026 the cabinet also invoked 'constructive abstention' on European Peace Facility financing of new lethal weapons for Ukraine, saying Bulgaria's mandatory contribution would be used only for non-lethal assistance. The decision does not cover commercial exports: Bulgaria's defence industry remains a supplier of ammunition destined for Ukraine, which the Defence Ministry says it does not control.
key_evidence: 10 June 2026: Radev announces the end of weapons supplies from army stocks; Stoyanov: 'There is nothing more we can give'
Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova: any future military-technical or humanitarian support will require a Council of Ministers decision and a debate in parliament
Euronews: the defence industry 'is set to remain one of the main suppliers of ammunition destined for Kyiv'
21 October 2026: constructive abstention on the European Peace Facility; contribution limited to non-lethal aid

title: Have Patriarch Kirill removed from the EU's next Russia sanctions package
description: On 18 June 2026, before a European Council summit, Radev said: 'Bulgaria will ask Patriarch Kirill to be removed from the sanction package', referring to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, who had been shielded from earlier EU listings by Hungary.
reasoning: In July 2026 Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said Bulgaria's reservations had been taken into account: Patriarch Kirill and Lukoil founder Vagit Alekperov were no longer in the proposed 21st sanctions package, as was a Russian citizen linked to spare parts for the Sofia metro, and Bulgaria was ready to support the package. At that point final adoption still depended on objections from other member states (Greece on energy, Austria on financial measures).
key_evidence: 18 June 2026: Radev announces Bulgaria will seek Kirill's removal
July 2026: Petrova confirms Kirill and Alekperov removed from the proposal; Bulgaria backs the package
Radev on Kirill: 'the time of crusades' is over; on Alekperov: supporting sanctions would mean 'shooting ourselves in the foot'

title: Renegotiate the Botas gas agreement with Türkiye
description: On 12 June 2026 Radev said, after meeting Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, that Ankara was interested in renegotiating the 2023 Bulgargaz–BOTAS agreement; Energy Minister Iva Petrova said she expected it to be 'fully renegotiated within one or two months'. The 13-year take-or-pay deal commits Bulgargaz to about BGN 1 million a day for LNG terminal capacity until 2035.
reasoning: After Radev's talks with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Ankara on 6 July 2026, Bulgargaz and BOTAS signed a protocol suspending the agreement for 15 months, during which Bulgaria pays only for capacity it actually uses under improved terms, and agreed to work towards renegotiating the contract. Radev said arrears had reached about USD 360 million because nothing had been paid since July 2024, and that settling them would not burden public finances. The renegotiated contract had not been reported concluded as of the latest reports found (August 2026), and the opposition asked what Bulgaria had conceded in return.
key_evidence: 12 June 2026: Radev says Türkiye is interested in renegotiation; Petrova expects it within one or two months
6 July 2026: protocol freezing the agreement for 15 months; renegotiation 'in line with current market conditions'
Radev: 'In the next 15 months, we will not pay for capacity. We will pay only for gas delivered through Botas'
Democratic Bulgaria's Ivaylo Mirchev questioned the terms; GERB's Temenuzhka Petkova noted the 15-month period coincides with local elections

title: Speed up completion of the National Children's Hospital
description: At the first cabinet meeting on 8 May 2026 Radev named 'the speedier completion of the National Pediatric Hospital' in Sofia as one of the government's healthcare priorities.
reasoning: The 2026 budget adopted on 24 July did not provide funding for the hospital's construction, which the opposition criticised. Health Minister Katya Ivkova said the same day that the procurement for the design and author supervision, launched in March 2026, had been challenged and suspended pending a court ruling, that more than EUR 46 million for the design sits in the budget of the state Health Investment Company, that no construction funds were needed in 2026 and that the ministry would take steps to regain control of the process. No construction step was found as of October 2026; the delay stems from a procurement dispute that predates the government.
key_evidence: 8 May 2026: speedier completion of the hospital named a healthcare priority
24 July 2026: opposition says the budget does not fund construction of the National Children's Hospital
24 July 2026: Ivkova: 'Under no circumstances is the government abandoning the construction'; design tender suspended in court

title: Speed up the modernisation of the Bulgarian Army
description: On 8 May 2026 Radev 'emphasized the need to speed up the modernization of the Bulgarian Army'. The governance programme's defence chapter lists modernisation of equipment and weaponry, investment in defence infrastructure and new technologies 'with a high asymmetric impact'.
reasoning: On 10 June 2026 parliament approved, by 186 votes to 3, the government's project to buy seven 3D radars from Thales (EUR 114.1 million, up to EUR 195 million) financed from the EU's SAFE loans; the 2026 budget allows up to EUR 3.261 billion of SAFE borrowing and the 2027 plan provides for investment in counter-drone and air-defence systems. Against this, the 2026 deficit forecast was lowered partly because of 'changes to military equipment delivery schedules', and on 22 October 2026 the European Parliament urged Bulgaria to stop delaying its participation in NATO's anti-drone initiative. Concrete steps exist, but the overall pace is mixed.
key_evidence: 10 June 2026: parliament approves seven Thales 3D radars, 186–3, financed under SAFE
2026 budget: up to EUR 3.261 billion of new borrowing under SAFE
15 October 2026: 2027 plan funds counter-drone and air-defence capabilities; 2026 deficit revision reflects revised Defence Ministry delivery schedules
22 October 2026: European Parliament resolution urges Bulgaria to stop delaying participation in NATO's lower-level air threats initiative
